paragraphs: MEG and EEG measure brain activity with millisecond timing, making them useful for studying how brain regions interact over time. However, reconstructing activity inside the brain from these measurements is underdetermined: the observations do not uniquely specify the underlying sources. A common approach first estimates each region's activity using independence assumptions, then analyzes relationships between the reconstructed signals.

This paper combines those stages in a state-space model. Average activity within each region becomes an internal state, while time-varying autoregression describes how regional activities depend on earlier activity across regions. This lets source estimation and changing connectivity participate in the same model, rather than estimating sources under assumptions that separate the regions before examining their dependence.

In simulations satisfying its assumptions, the model produced smaller estimation errors than minimum-norm source reconstruction followed by autoregression. Results from one participant's scene-processing MEG data were preliminary: they suggested leading and lagged linear relationships between early visual cortex and a scene-sensitive region. Those relationships could reflect forward and feedback information flow, rather than establishing that interpretation conclusively.
neurips-2016-a-state-space-model-of-cros.tldr: A joint state-space model improves connectivity estimates in simulations satisfying its assumptions and offers preliminary evidence of changing visual-region dependencies.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose actions adaptively while respecting a budget and judging performance by the worst case. In an adaptive procedure, information revealed by earlier choices can influence later decisions. The question is whether simple greedy rules can come close to the best achievable utility when each action also consumes resources.

The analysis covers both modular costs and non-modular costs, allowing the cost structure to be more complicated than adding independent charges. For each setting, the authors show that two simple greedy algorithms can individually fail to be near-optimal. Nevertheless, choosing the better of their results has a near-optimality guarantee under the corresponding assumption: pointwise submodularity or pointwise cost-sensitive submodularity.

The budget comparison is essential to interpreting that guarantee. The combined procedure is compared with an optimal algorithm using half the budget, rather than an unrestricted optimum using the same resources. The paper also discusses applications and compares the greedy procedures experimentally on active learning. Its central contribution is a conditional guarantee explaining how two individually inadequate rules can complement each other.
neurips-2016-adaptive-maximization-of-po.tldr: Selecting the better of two greedy procedures gives a conditional near-optimality guarantee against an optimum using half the budget.

paragraphs: Ada Newton addresses large-scale empirical risk minimization by growing the training sample during optimization. Its target is statistical accuracy: solving each sample-based problem to the precision warranted by that sample. This shifts attention from repeatedly optimizing the full dataset to coordinating the amount of data with the progress of the optimizer.

The key is to enlarge the sample while keeping the current solution close enough to the next problem's optimum. In that local neighborhood, Newton's method can exploit quadratic convergence. The authors show theoretically how successive sample increases and single Newton updates can remain within the statistical accuracy of the regularized empirical risk, without requiring a line search at each stage.

Doubling the sample is supported when the number of observations is sufficiently large; it is not presented as an unconditional rule for every starting sample. Experiments on several datasets support doubling at each iteration. Under that progression, the authors report reaching the full dataset's statistical accuracy with about two passes over the data, connecting the convergence argument to reduced data-processing work.
neurips-2016-adaptive-newton-method-for-.tldr: Ada Newton grows its training sample so single Newton updates can track statistical accuracy, enabling about two data passes in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Online multi-task learning must update several related prediction problems as observations arrive. The challenge here is twofold: learn a model for each task while also learning how the tasks relate to one another. The relationships matter because they determine how information from one task can contribute to learning another.

The proposed algorithm handles both parts jointly and gives the procedure a probabilistic interpretation. Its update rules are designed to be efficient, and it allows flexible control over how much learners emphasize their own task versus learning across all tasks. This makes the balance between specialization and shared learning an explicit part of the approach.

The authors prove a sublinear regret bound relative to the best linear predictor chosen in hindsight. In that comparison, the accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average contribution diminishes. Experiments on three multi-task benchmark datasets show advantages over several leading online multi-task baselines. These results support the combination of adaptive task relationships and efficient online updates in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2016-adaptive-smoothed-online-mu.tldr: An online algorithm jointly learns task models and their relationships, with sublinear regret and favorable results on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of a noisy function whose evaluations may be expensive. Hyperparameter tuning is one example: evaluating a candidate can require training a model. Sequential methods choose one setting at a time, which limits their ability to use facilities that can evaluate many candidates simultaneously.

The paper proposes selecting batches through determinantal point processes, or DPPs. These model diversity within a set, making the relationships among proposed evaluations part of batch construction. Their kernels are learned automatically. The central idea is that a useful parallel batch should account for how its candidates relate to one another, instead of treating each proposed evaluation as an isolated choice.

The authors generalize an earlier theoretical result and establish improved regret bounds based on DPP sampling. They also evaluate the approach on synthetic functions, robotics tasks, and hyperparameter optimization. Those experiments indicate that the DPP methods outperform the compared state-of-the-art methods, particularly when batches are sampled from the DPP. The contribution combines an explicit model of batch diversity with theoretical and empirical support for parallel search.
neurips-2016-batched-gaussian-process-ba.tldr: Automatically learned determinantal point processes select diverse evaluation batches, improving regret bounds and reported Bayesian optimization performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much damage malicious training data can cause when the attacker knows very little. The attacker cannot inspect the learner's training set and does not know any parameter of the distribution generating it. The issue is whether this lack of information still permits attacks with provable consequences for learning.

The authors construct simple data-injection attacks under two different assumptions about the learner's knowledge. An informed learner knows the attacker's chosen strategy. A blind learner knows only the fraction of malicious observations and a family containing the attacker's malicious distribution. These settings separate the attacker's limited information from the information available to the defender.

For each attack, the analysis establishes lower bounds on minimax risk and examines convergence rates. These bounds describe unavoidable worst-case estimation difficulty, rather than merely showing that a particular learning algorithm performs poorly. The examples demonstrate that an attacker need not observe the training data to create fundamental obstacles to learning. They also show why knowing the attack strategy and knowing only its broad characteristics are meaningfully different defensive settings.
neurips-2016-blind-attacks-on-machine-le.tldr: Simple data-injection attacks can impose provable learning limits even without access to training data or distribution parameters.

paragraphs: The paper uses deep convolutional neural networks to model how retinal cells respond to natural scenes. Such responses are difficult to capture because sensory circuits contain multiple layers and nonlinear processes. The reported predictions approach the variability of a cell's own responses and are substantially more accurate than linear-nonlinear models and generalized linear models.

The networks also show advantages beyond prediction accuracy on the original stimulus distribution. With small training datasets, they are less susceptible to overfitting than the linear-nonlinear models. They also generalize better across different stimulus distributions, including natural scenes and white noise. Examining their learned representations shows that natural scenes require a richer collection of feature maps than white noise.

The authors further connect model behavior to candidate circuit mechanisms. Feedforward inhibition produces precisely timed responses to slowly changing inputs. Adding hidden noise sources helps capture unusually low spike-count variability, while recurrent lateral connections allow contrast adaptation to emerge. These findings make the models useful as tools for investigating internal computation as well as predicting responses; the abstract presents the methods as extendable to other sensory settings.
neurips-2016-deep-learning-models-of-the.tldr: Deep CNNs accurately model retinal responses to natural scenes and reveal model mechanisms associated with timing, variability, and contrast adaptation.

paragraphs: The exponential mechanism provides a general route to randomized estimation with pure differential privacy, expressed as (ε, 0)-privacy. The abstract describes a connection between that mechanism and Gibbs posteriors, a class of data-dependent probability distributions that includes Bayesian posteriors. The earlier connection relies on boundedness conditions on the loss function.

Those conditions can be restrictive for learning problems whose losses do not fit the required bounds. This paper instead studies Gibbs posteriors under convex and Lipschitz losses and targets (ε, δ)-differential privacy. The additional δ changes the privacy guarantee being sought, so the extension should be understood together with that change rather than as the same pure-privacy result under weaker assumptions.

The stated result permits loss functions with unbounded sensitivity, extending the reach of the classical exponential-mechanism framework. The important distinction is between removing a bounded-sensitivity requirement and removing all restrictions on the loss: convexity and the Lipschitz condition remain part of the setting studied. The contribution is a theoretical route to privacy for a broader class of losses through Gibbs-posterior estimation.
neurips-2016-differential-privacy-withou.tldr: The paper establishes approximate differential privacy for Gibbs posteriors with convex, Lipschitz losses that may have unbounded sensitivity.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from comparisons between pairs of options. Double Thompson Sampling, or D-TS, uses posterior sampling to select both members of each comparison. It maintains uncertainty over a preference matrix and draws two independent sets of samples from that posterior to guide the two choices.

The method applies to general Copeland dueling bandits, with Condorcet problems included as a special case. For K options and T rounds, the authors prove regret of order K² log T in the general setting. A refined argument gives order K log T plus K² log log T for Condorcet problems and many practical Copeland problems. The stronger bound therefore applies to a specified subset of settings.

The paper also introduces D-TS+, which uses careful tie-breaking to reduce regret. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data report significant improvements in both regret and robustness for the proposed methods. The appeal is that a simple selection principle—independent posterior sampling for each candidate—supports broad applicability, while the analysis identifies cases where the regret dependence can be substantially sharper.
neurips-2016-double-thompson-sampling-fo.tldr: Double Thompson Sampling chooses both comparison candidates through independent posterior draws and achieves regret guarantees across general dueling-bandit settings.

paragraphs: Inspired by horseshoe-bat echolocation, this paper develops a spiking neural circuit for detecting a target's horizontal direction. The circuit becomes part of a navigation and target-tracking model. It uses a simple sensor based on local information, with a cardioid-shaped angular response, and can operate at a biological firing rate of 10 Hz.

At that rate, the network tracks large angular targets of 60 degrees within one second, with a reported 10% root-mean-square error. The authors also study foraging and target localization among obstacles. With 50% additive noise, they report only a 1% performance loss relative to a proportional-integral-derivative controller, while requiring substantially fewer spike-triggered decisions.

Increasing the average spike rate to 100 Hz or 1000 Hz yields better performance. Even at those accelerated rates, the reported decision counts remain 20-fold and 10-fold lower, respectively. The findings connect the biological inspiration to a concrete computational trade-off: sparse spike-driven decisions can support navigation under noise, while higher firing rates offer another operating point when stronger performance is desired.
neurips-2016-efficient-and-robust-spikin.tldr: A bat-inspired spiking circuit supports noisy target tracking and navigation with substantially fewer decisions than a conventional controller.

paragraphs: This paper approaches topic learning through the geometry underlying Latent Dirichlet Allocation and its nonparametric extensions. Instead of directly optimizing the LDA likelihood, it studies a geometric loss that serves as a substitute objective. This makes the geometric structure of topics the basis for both learning and inference.

The resulting algorithm combines an efficient weighted-clustering procedure with geometric corrections. Clustering provides the main optimization step, while the corrections incorporate the topic model's geometry. The authors present this combination as a way to overcome computational and statistical inefficiencies associated with techniques based on Gibbs sampling and variational inference, while retaining accuracy comparable to a Gibbs sampler.

The paper also establishes statistical consistency of its topic estimates under specified conditions. That is a conditional theoretical result, complementing the practical motivation for faster inference. Extensive experiments on simulated and real data evaluate the method. Together, the contributions show how replacing a likelihood with a geometrically motivated surrogate can produce an efficient topic-learning procedure with both accuracy evidence and a consistency guarantee.
neurips-2016-geometric-dirichlet-means-a.tldr: Geometric Dirichlet Means combines weighted clustering and geometric corrections for efficient topic inference with conditional statistical consistency.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical theory of hierarchical graph clustering. A hierarchy describes groups at multiple levels, so evaluating a clustering algorithm requires a target that captures more than one partition. The authors address this foundational question by defining what it means for a graph-clustering hierarchy to be correct.

Their modeling assumption is that the observed graph is sampled from a graphon. The abstract describes graphons as a general framework for generating graphs and studying large networks, richer than stochastic block models. This broadens the modeling setting beyond the block-model framework that had supported much of the statistical theory of graph clustering.

Within that setting, the authors provide sufficient conditions for statistical consistency and give an explicit algorithm satisfying them. The conditions establish a route to correctness; they are not presented as requirements that every successful algorithm must obey. The contribution connects three pieces that need to agree: a graph-generating model, a definition of the desired hierarchy, and a procedure with a corresponding statistical guarantee.
neurips-2016-graphons-mergeons-and-so-on.tldr: The paper defines correct hierarchical clustering for graphon-generated graphs and supplies an algorithm satisfying sufficient conditions for consistency.

paragraphs: Guided policy search trains a complex policy by supervised imitation of a teacher, such as a trajectory optimizer. This avoids directly computing policy gradients in a large parameter space. Existing methods offer asymptotic local convergence guarantees, but those guarantees do not by themselves explain how much improvement occurs within a small number of iterations.

The paper interprets guided policy search as approximate mirror descent. In this view, the projection onto the relevant constraint manifold is imperfect. Making that approximation explicit gives the authors a way to analyze its consequences and derive a simpler guided policy search algorithm.

The new algorithm has improvement and convergence guarantees in simplified convex and linear settings. For the broader nonlinear setting, the authors instead show that projection error can be bounded. Simulated robotic manipulation experiments find stable behavior and performance similar to or better than earlier guided policy search methods, with fewer hyperparameters. The significance is both conceptual and practical: an optimization interpretation clarifies the source of approximation while supporting a simpler training procedure.
neurips-2016-guided-policy-search-via-ap.tldr: Viewing guided policy search as approximate mirror descent yields a simpler algorithm with qualified guarantees and favorable simulated robotics results.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires identifying image evidence that addresses a question. Attention models often handle this by highlighting relevant image regions. This paper argues that selecting the relevant parts of the question is equally important: the model needs to determine which language information should guide its interpretation of the image.

The proposed co-attention model reasons jointly about attention over the image and the question. It also processes the question hierarchically using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network. Through co-attention, that hierarchy influences image reasoning as well. The approach therefore connects language selection and visual selection instead of treating the question only as a fixed instruction for locating image regions.

The reported VQA result increases from 60.3% to 60.5%, while COCO-QA increases from 61.6% to 63.3%. Using ResNet raises the reported results further to 62.1% and 65.4%, respectively. These benchmark findings support the usefulness of joint question-image attention, with different improvement sizes across the datasets and an additional benefit reported when ResNet is used.
neurips-2016-hierarchical-question-image.tldr: Hierarchical co-attention jointly selects relevant question content and image regions, improving reported visual question answering results.

paragraphs: The paper tackles missing-data recovery and clustering together for high-dimensional observations lying in a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Its organizing idea is self-expression: complete the data so each point can be reconstructed from a small number of other points using linear or affine combinations. This structure can remain useful even when the entire data matrix has high rank.

Because the resulting problem is NP-hard, the authors introduce a lifting framework that turns it into group-sparse recovery with rank-one constraints. They propose both a rank-pursuit algorithm and a convex relaxation. The resulting solutions fill in missing entries and produce a similarity matrix that can be used for clustering.

The methods handle low- and high-rank matrices without requiring subspace dimensions in advance, and the authors report freedom from initialization problems and applicability with few observations. Experiments include synthetic data, video motion segmentation, and motion-capture completion. Performance matches or exceeds low-rank completion methods when the matrix is low rank and substantially exceeds existing algorithms on the evaluated high-rank data.
neurips-2016-high-rank-matrix-completion.tldr: Self-expressive subspace structure enables joint matrix completion and clustering even when the overall data matrix has high rank.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a biologically plausible neural implementation of approximate probabilistic inference. It uses probabilistic population codes, where distributed neural activity represents probability distributions. Connecting several such codes through a graphical model lets the network represent uncertainty about multiple variables and combine evidence across their relationships.

Loopy belief propagation offers an attractive computational starting point because it spreads local information through a graph using marginalization and evidence integration. However, the authors identify a feature that makes its direct neural implementation implausible. They instead use an equivalent formulation based on tree-based reparameterizations, then express those updates as a nonlinear dynamical system with fast and slow timescales.

Combining that dynamical system with population codes yields the proposed inference network. Simulations on Gaussian graphical models show inference quality comparable to directly evaluating loopy belief propagation, together with robustness to noise. These results support the network as a possible mechanism for probabilistic computation in the brain. The evidence establishes a promising implementation in the simulated setting, rather than demonstrating that biological brains use this particular procedure.
neurips-2016-inference-by-reparameteriza.tldr: Reformulating belief propagation as fast-and-slow neural dynamics enables a biologically plausible population-code implementation of approximate inference.

paragraphs: Learned region sparsity makes image-level decisions using a small set of local regions. The paper connects this selective use of visual information to how people move their eyes while making decisions. It asks whether a model built for classification can also account for where people look during visual search.

The authors add Inhibition of Return, a biologically plausible attention mechanism, to encourage diversity among the selected regions. Sparsity controls how much local information is used, while diversity encourages the selected set to cover different regions. The resulting model is tested on three types of visual search task to examine how these two mechanisms relate to human attention.

The model achieves reported state-of-the-art performance in predicting gaze fixation locations despite training only with image-level labels and no object-location annotations. Its classification performance remains unchanged from the original model. The findings suggest that selective, diverse region use can explain aspects of gaze behavior while preserving classification ability, linking an attention-inspired modification to both visual prediction and a computational account of human information sampling.
neurips-2016-learned-region-sparsity-and.tldr: Adding diversity to sparse region selection predicts human gaze from image-level training labels while preserving classification performance.

paragraphs: The paper aims to help deep networks generalize while making their learned representations easier to interpret. It approaches both goals through parsimony: encouraging representations to have a more economical organization. The proposed tool is a clustering-based regularizer, which adds a preference for clustered structure to the learning objective.

The regularization objective follows the style of k-means and is described as easy to optimize. It supports several forms of organization, including clustering across samples, spatial clustering, and co-clustering. This flexibility matters because the same broad principle can be applied to different aspects of a learned representation, rather than being tied to only one arrangement of the data.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on unsupervised learning, classification, fine-grained categorization, and zero-shot learning. The range of tasks supports the usefulness of clustering as a representation-learning constraint across different learning settings. The central contribution is the regularization approach itself: an optimizable way to encourage structured, economical representations in pursuit of better generalization and interpretability, with empirical demonstrations across the listed tasks.
neurips-2016-learning-deep-parsimonious-.tldr: A flexible k-means-style regularizer encourages economical deep representations, with demonstrations across several learning tasks.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent words as vectors that other language-processing systems can reuse. This paper shows that embeddings trained on Google News contain substantial female/male gender stereotypes. Because downstream applications use those representations, the authors argue that applying them without examining their associations can amplify biases already present in the training material.

The method uses two geometric observations: gender bias is captured by a direction in the embedding, and gender-neutral words are linearly separable from words whose definitions involve gender. These properties guide changes intended to remove stereotypical associations while retaining meaningful ones. The aim is to change associations such as receptionist with female while preserving associations such as queen with female.

Crowd-worker evaluations and standard benchmarks show significant empirical reductions in gender bias while maintaining useful capabilities, including grouping related concepts and solving analogies. The result demonstrates that modifying embedding geometry can address the targeted stereotypes without discarding those measured semantic abilities. The authors present the modified embeddings as a way for applications to use these representations without amplifying the gender bias they address.
neurips-2016-man-is-to-computer-programm.tldr: Geometric modifications reduce measured gender stereotypes in word embeddings while preserving meaningful gender associations and tested semantic capabilities.

paragraphs: Training recurrent neural networks with backpropagation through time requires managing intermediate results across a sequence. Keeping those results available consumes memory, while recreating them later consumes computation. This paper treats the choice between storage and recomputation as an optimization problem governed by a user-selected memory budget.

The proposed algorithm uses dynamic programming to choose an execution policy that minimizes computational cost within that budget. It can fit tightly within almost any specified memory allowance. This makes available device memory an explicit input to the training schedule, allowing the procedure to determine which intermediate results are worth retaining and which should be recomputed.

The authors provide asymptotic upper bounds on computation for several regimes and report particular benefits for long sequences. For sequences of length 1000, the method reduces memory use by 95% while increasing time per iteration by only one third relative to standard backpropagation through time. That example illustrates a substantial memory reduction at a measured computational cost, rather than a claim that memory savings come without extra work.
neurips-2016-memory-efficient-backpropag.tldr: Dynamic programming optimizes storage and recomputation for recurrent-network training under a user-set memory budget.

paragraphs: Graph reconstruction learns a rule for predicting connections between data points. The paper considers empirical risk minimization over every possible pair of nodes in a training graph. For n nodes, that objective averages prediction error across n(n−1)/2 pairs, directly linking the learning problem to a potentially expensive pairwise computation.

The first contribution is a learning rate of order log n divided by n, improving on the earlier order 1/√n rate described in the abstract. The authors characterize these fast rates as universal within the studied problem. Unlike comparable fast-rate results in several other learning settings, they do not depend on strong assumptions about the data distribution.

The second contribution examines whether the statistical benefit can survive a cheaper objective. Instead of processing every pair, a Monte Carlo version samples B pairs with replacement, where B is much smaller than n². The authors investigate how much this substitution can preserve the learning rates and illustrate the theory on synthetic and real graphs. The work therefore addresses statistical accuracy and the computational burden of learning from large graphs together.
neurips-2016-on-graph-reconstruction-via.tldr: The paper proves fast graph-reconstruction learning rates and studies whether sampling node pairs can preserve them at lower computational cost.

paragraphs: The labeled stochastic block model describes items in hidden clusters, with a random label observed for every pair. Label probabilities depend on the clusters containing the two items, and pair labels are generated independently. The paper assumes finitely many clusters, each growing linearly with the total population, and seeks to recover their memberships from the labels.

Rather than considering only exact recovery or a vanishing fraction of errors, the authors characterize when an algorithm can achieve at most s misclassified items on average for any s=o(n). This specifies an error target that grows more slowly than the population. It gives a finer account of recovery difficulty by connecting model parameters to a chosen average error allowance.

The paper also develops an algorithm based on simple spectral methods that reaches the fundamental performance limit. Its computation is O(n polylog(n)), and it does not require the model parameters in advance. The contribution therefore combines a characterization of what recovery accuracy is achievable with an efficient procedure attaining that limit under the stated model.
neurips-2016-optimal-cluster-recovery-in.tldr: The paper characterizes attainable average clustering errors in labeled block models and gives an efficient spectral algorithm achieving that limit.

paragraphs: Adaptive gradient methods use past gradients to adjust optimization steps. The common diagonal form of AdaGrad tracks information separately for each coordinate. Full-matrix AdaGrad can also capture dependencies between features and may perform better in some situations, but its computational requirements become impractical in high-dimensional problems.

The paper introduces Ada-LR and RadaGrad, two approximations based on randomized dimensionality reduction. They aim to retain useful cross-feature information while reducing the cost of full-matrix adaptation. The theoretical analysis shows that Ada-LR's regret is close to that of full-matrix AdaGrad, whose dependence on dimension can be up to exponentially smaller than the diagonal variant's.

Experiments find that both approximations perform similarly to full-matrix AdaGrad at substantially lower computational cost. In convolutional and recurrent neural-network training, RadaGrad converges faster than diagonal AdaGrad in the reported evaluations. These findings support random projection as a practical way to preserve benefits of richer adaptive updates. The strongest dimensional advantage remains a possibility in favorable situations, rather than a guarantee that full-matrix information always produces that improvement.
neurips-2016-scalable-adaptive-stochasti.tldr: Randomized low-dimensional approximations retain full-matrix AdaGrad's feature dependencies at lower cost, with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: The paper questions a common separation in neural networks between rapidly changing neural activities and slowly learned connection weights. Activities represent current or recent inputs, while ordinary weights capture longer-term regularities. The authors argue that this leaves room for another timescale, motivated by the varied dynamics of biological synapses.

Their proposal is to use fast weights: variables that change more slowly than neural activities but much more quickly than standard learned weights. These weights hold temporary memories of recent experience. The distinction concerns the role and lifetime of stored information, allowing recent history to influence processing through changing connections rather than only through ongoing activity.

Fast weights provide a neurally plausible implementation of attention to the recent past, of the kind useful in sequence-to-sequence models. The authors also state that this approach avoids storing copies of neural activity patterns. The contribution is an alternative memory mechanism: temporary information resides in rapidly adapting weights, connecting attention over recent experience with a broader view of the timescales available to neural computation.
neurips-2016-using-fast-weights-to-atten.tldr: Fast-changing weights store temporary memories and implement attention to recent experience without retaining copies of neural activity patterns.

paragraphs: Yggdrasil addresses the cost of training deep decision trees across multiple machines. The abstract identifies poor scaling in the PLANET approach as feature dimensionality and tree depth increase. Yggdrasil changes how data and computation are organized, partitioning data by feature and combining that layout with specialized training data structures.

The system trains directly on compressed features and labels when they are compressible, and supplies efficient structures for uncompressed data as well. Sparse bitvectors reduce communication among machines. It also avoids requiring feature binning for split selection, whereas PLANET uses binning to approximate split points. The authors analytically examine the effect of that approximation.

The paper reports speedups of up to 24-fold over existing methods overall. Evaluations on MNIST 8M and a high-dimensional Yahoo dataset show speedups of up to an order of magnitude on both datasets. These are reported upper-end improvements in the evaluated comparisons. The contribution shows how feature-based partitioning, compressed-data processing, and reduced communication can jointly improve distributed tree training as data dimensionality and tree depth grow.
neurips-2016-yggdrasil-an-optimized-syst.tldr: Yggdrasil accelerates distributed deep-tree training through feature-based partitioning, optimized storage, and lower communication costs.
